definition: One place OCX discovers settings: the system, user, OCX home or managed tier. A later tier overrides an earlier one.
The registry name OCX puts in front of an identifier that names none: `ocx.sh` unless configured otherwise.
`OCX_NO_CONFIG=1`, which skips discovered config files and the managed config; locked system-tier sections and explicitly named files still load.
An ordered list of sources OCX checks strongest first for one setting or credential; the first match wins.
Corporate settings published as an ordinary OCX package. Each host keeps a synced copy and layers it over its config files.
A `[mirrors]` entry that sends all traffic for one registry host to a replacement endpoint, with no fallback to the origin.
The person who configures OCX on many hosts and publishes the patches or managed config they use.
A package together with all its transitive dependencies, which composition walks deepest first.
Building one runtime environment from the environment entries of a package and its dependencies, in dependency order.
The `visibility` of one dependency, choosing which of that dependency's surfaces reach the package that depends on it.
The `visibility` of one environment entry in package metadata, choosing the surfaces it joins.
The reverse-DNS name that keys one entry in a package's `integrations` block, such as `com.microsoft.vscode`. OCX does not enforce the shape.
The part of a package's environment that consumers see when they run the package or depend on it.
The part of a package's environment that only its own launchers see at run time, selected with `--self`.
The rule that global toolchain packages never compose into, supplement or replace a project's resolved environment.
An order in which every dependency comes before the packages that need it.
Which surface an environment entry or a dependency reaches: the interface surface, the private surface, both or neither.
Publish a package's registry tags into its index entry, as a change request on the index repository.
Register a package in an index for the first time, through a reviewed change request. The claimed unit is the package.
The image index a tag resolved to, stored verbatim in the local index under its own digest.
A mode, set by `--frozen` or `OCX_FROZEN`, in which tags resolve only from the local index and an unknown tag fails.
A catalog that maps each package's tags to digests, so OCX can choose a version without asking the registry.
The Git repository on a forge that stores an index's files; claims and announcements arrive there as change requests.
A digest-named `__ocx.keep` tag a push writes for each platform manifest, so a deleted tag cannot leave the manifest unreachable.
A copy of an index under the OCX home, recording what this host last resolved. It changes only when a command refreshes it.
A mode, set by `--offline`, in which OCX makes no network request at all and fails on anything not already local.
A `login:id` pair in a root document that may announce the package; the numeric `id` is the half that counts.
`index.ocx.sh`, the hosted index for the `ocx.sh` registry name; it points each package at the registry that stores it.
The live source a resolve queries over the network: the registry itself, or an index service such as `index.ocx.sh`.
A package's top-level entry in an index: its repository pointer, tags, owners and declared publishers.
A local index subtree packaged inside a tool release and selected with `OCX_INDEX`, so that tool resolves offline.
A publisher's mark on a tag that OCX refuses to install by default; the tag itself stays in the registry.
A short, stable machine-readable name for a failure cause, carried in an error document's `error.detail`.
The JSON object a failing command prints on stdout under `--format json`, naming the exit code and a detail slug.
A key-value string on an OCI manifest, such as `org.opencontainers.image.source`, that tools and catalogs read.
Any content a registry stores by digest: a layer archive, a config or a manifest.
Stored under a name derived from the content's own digest, so identical bytes are stored once and never change in place.
A small JSON record inside an OCI manifest that names other content by media type, digest and size.
A SHA-256 hash of exact bytes, written `sha256:<hex>`; unlike a tag, it names one piece of content forever.
The `sha256-<hex>` tag that holds referrers on a registry without the Referrers API.
The string that names a package, `registry/repository[:tag][@digest]`, with the default registry filled in when omitted.
An OCI manifest that lists one platform manifest per platform under a single tag, so each host picks its own build.
One archive of files in a manifest, addressed by its digest; OCX extracts each layer once and shares it between packages.
An OCI JSON document that describes one stored artifact: its config and its layers, each by digest.
The path segments of a repository before the package name, such as `acme` in `ocx.sh/acme/widget`.
The Open Container Initiative, whose specifications define the registry protocol and artifact formats OCX stores packages in.
The manifest of one platform's build, listed in an image index; dependency pins and lock entries name its digest.
An artifact, such as a signature or SBOM, that names another manifest as its subject, so a registry lists it beside that manifest.
A server that speaks the OCI distribution protocol and stores repositories of tags, manifests and blobs, such as GHCR or Docker Hub.
The first segment of an identifier, such as `ocx.sh`; a mirror or the public index may route it to another storage host.
A named collection of tags and manifests inside a registry, such as `nodejs/node`; one repository holds one package.
A mutable, human-readable name in a repository, such as `3.28` or `latest`, that points at one manifest digest.

definition: A link inside a package's `refs/` directory that records who uses the package, so garbage collection keeps it.
A symlink at `symlinks/<registry>/<repo>/candidates/<tag>`, created by install, that keeps one installed version of a package reachable.
A package that a patch descriptor names, whose environment entries OCX layers onto every matching target package.
The one symlink per repository that points at the selected candidate; `ocx package select` and `install --select` move it.
A package whose download waits until one of its commands first runs, chosen with the `lazy-mode` key.
A named command a package declares in its metadata; OCX generates a launcher for it so the command runs from `PATH`.
One JSON file OCX writes just before it starts a binary, naming each package's manifest digest and the environment inputs of that launch.
The sweep `ocx clean` runs: it deletes every stored object that no symlink, project lock or dependency still reaches.
Download a package into the object store. `ocx package install` also creates its candidate symlink; project commands such as `ocx add` install without one.

definition: A generated native executable that starts a program from the record `NAME.launch` beside it; the record's `kind` says whether it starts a package entry point, a deferred tool, a toolchain tool or a vendored program.
One route into OCX that writes an execution record: `exec`, `package exec`, `launcher exec` or a shim.
Make a package's files present on disk by downloading and extracting its layers into the object store.
The compiled program every launcher is on every OS, one shared blob copied under each name, with its record `NAME.launch` beside it.
The content-addressed directories under the OCX home that hold every downloaded blob, extracted layer and assembled package, keyed by digest.
The directory where OCX keeps its stores, local index, state and global toolchain: `$OCX_HOME`, or `~/.ocx` when unset.
A versioned set of pre-built files plus metadata, stored as OCI artifacts in a registry and installed by OCX as one unit.

definition: The `metadata.json` document a package carries: how OCX extracts it, its environment entries, dependencies and entry points.
The directory of one assembled package in the object store; its `content/` subdirectory holds the package's files.
An operator-published overlay that changes the environment a package runs in, without changing the package itself.
A small JSON document in a registry that names which companion packages apply to which target packages.
The file `ocx patch freeze` writes, pinning every patch to an exact digest for reproducible builds.
Fix a reference to one exact value, such as a tag to a digest or a trust policy to one signer identity.
The launcher of a deferred package (record kind `deferred`); its first run downloads the package, then starts the real binary.
A file stored next to an archive or blob to carry its metadata, such as the `metadata.json` beside a bundle.
The directory that receives execution records; configuring one is what turns recording on.
A generated executable in a toolchain tree's `active/bin` that re-enters `ocx exec` against its own project when it runs.
Apple Mobile File Integrity, the macOS kernel module that checks code signatures independently of Gatekeeper.
The platform `any`: a build with no platform requirement, used where no exact platform match exists.
A macOS seal embedded in a binary; Apple silicon refuses to run a binary whose signature does not match its bytes.
The OCI `platform.variant` field, a CPU sub-architecture such as `v8` for `arm64`; unrelated to package variants.
The program, such as `ld-linux.so` or the musl loader, that loads a dynamically linked Linux binary and its libraries.
The macOS check that stops downloaded apps and binaries without an approved signature from running.
An Alpine package that lets some glibc binaries run on musl; the loader is still musl's own.
The GNU C Library, the libc of Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and most other Linux distributions.
The C library a Linux binary links against, glibc or musl; OCX records the requirement as a libc feature.
The `libc.glibc` or `libc.musl` entry in a platform's `os.features`, stating the libc a Linux build requires.
The executable file format of macOS.
A small libc used by Alpine Linux and static builds; a glibc binary does not run on it without help.
The Windows variable listing the extensions a shell appends to a bare command name, such as `.EXE` and `.BAT`.
The operating system and CPU a build targets, written `os/arch`, optionally refined by a CPU variant and a libc feature.
The `com.apple.quarantine` attribute macOS sets on downloaded files, which makes Gatekeeper check them.
A binary that carries its libraries inside it and needs no libc from the host.
The WebAssembly System Interface; OCX gives each WASI version its own platform, such as `wasip1/wasm`.
Applying a toolchain to a shell, set per project by `activate`: `env` sets `PATH` and the package variables, `bin` only `PATH`, `none` nothing.
One entry in a `[tools]` table: a local name on the left, the identifier it resolves to on the right.
The user-wide `ocx.toml` and `ocx.lock` in the OCX home, reached only with `--global` and never mixed into a project.
A named subset of a project's bindings, declared as `[group.<name>.tools]`, so a host downloads only the tools it needs.
`ocx.lock`, written by `ocx lock` beside `ocx.toml`: it pins every binding to per-platform digests, so later commands skip the registry.
A directory tree whose root holds an `ocx.toml`; commands run inside it resolve against that file and its lock file.
The commands that read `ocx.toml` and `ocx.lock` and take binding names, such as `ocx add` and `ocx lock`. The `ocx package` commands take identifiers.
Write or refresh the toolchain tree from the lock file, as `ocx pull` and `ocx add` do.
A file under `$OCX_HOME/state/` that records which lock and entries a toolchain tree was last rendered from.
The set of bindings an `ocx.toml` declares, each a local name that resolves to one package.
The directory `<project>/.ocx/toolchain/` that OCX renders from the lock file: stable links and trampolines for every binding.
The `<stem>-receipt.json` file `ocx package create` writes beside a bundle, which `push` and `test` read back.
A tag with a `_build` suffix, such as `3.28.1_20260301`, that by convention the publisher never re-pushes.
The build output a publisher pushes: one archive of the package's files plus its metadata sidecar.
Moving a new release's rolling tags along with it, so pushing `3.28.1` also moves `3.28`, `3` and `latest`.
A pull request on GitHub or a merge request on GitLab: the form in which claims and announcements reach an index.
A Git hosting service such as GitHub or GitLab, where index repositories and their change requests live.
The README, logo, title and keywords attached to a repository with `ocx package description push`, stored as an OCI manifest.
Copy a package's platform manifests and blobs byte for byte from one repository to another with `ocx package copy`.
The person or CI job that builds a package and pushes it to a registry.
A tag such as `3.28`, `3` or `latest` that moves forward to the newest matching release.
Semantic Versioning: versions written `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, where each part signals breaking, additive or fix changes.
A pre-release tag meant to be deleted later, such as a canary or nightly, marked ephemeral when announced.
A small, deterministic, Python-like language; `ocx package test --script` runs package tests written in it.
One line of tags that cascade together, such as one variant's releases or a pre-release line like `0.5.0-canary`.
A build flavor of one package, such as `slim` or `debug`, published under a tag prefix like `slim-1.2.3`.
A Docker-style program that hands registry credentials to tools on request, configured in `~/.docker/config.json`.
Server-side request forgery: tricking a tool into contacting internal addresses for an attacker, which OCX guards against when following redirects.
The CA certificates OCX trusts for TLS: the compiled-in Mozilla roots plus the host's own store.
A file a CI runner reads to carry variables and `PATH` entries to later steps, such as GitHub's `GITHUB_ENV`; `ocx env --ci` appends to it.
Permission for the shell hook to activate a project; a fresh clone stays inert until a path grant, namespace grant or consent stamp covers it.
The file `ocx init`, `ocx add` and `ocx shell allow` write, recording which sources a project's lock file resolved against at consent.
One thin file per shell family, such as `$OCX_HOME/env.sh`, that `ocx self setup` writes and the shell profile sources.
The marked section OCX writes into a shell profile and later updates or removes, leaving the rest of the file untouched.
The login-session `PATH` entry `ocx self setup` registers, so IDEs and services that never read a shell profile still find OCX.
The per-prompt function OCX adds to a shell, which recomposes the environment, `PATH` and the package variables, after a `cd` or a lock change.
A signed statement about a package, such as provenance or an SBOM, bound to the exact manifest digest it describes.
Sigstore's command-line signing tool; OCX signatures and attestations interoperate with it.
A signer identity listed in a package's root document; OCX accepts its signatures as it would a matching trust policy.
Dead Simple Signing Envelope: the JSON wrapper that signs an attestation's payload together with its type.
Sigstore's certificate authority: it exchanges an OIDC token for a short-lived X.509 certificate naming the signer identity.
A supply-chain metadata framework; its statement format carries an attestation's subject digest and predicate.
Signing with a throwaway key whose certificate Fulcio binds to an OIDC identity, so no long-lived key exists.
OpenID Connect: the token standard CI systems and identity providers use to prove a signer's identity to Fulcio.
The body of an attestation: the document, such as an SBOM, whose bytes the in-toto statement wraps.
Package URL, a standard identifier string; execution records name packages as `pkg:oci` purls whose version is the digest.
Sigstore's append-only transparency log; each logged signature gets a Signed Entry Timestamp that verifiers check.
Subject Alternative Name: the certificate field that holds the signer identity, such as a workflow URL or an email address.
Software bill of materials: a list of the components inside a package, attached to it as a referrer.
Signed Certificate Timestamp: proof embedded in a Fulcio certificate that a certificate-transparency log recorded it.
Signed Entry Timestamp: Rekor's signed promise that a signature entered its transparency log at a given time.
The OIDC identity a signing certificate names, such as a CI workflow URL, which a trust policy pins.
An open signing service: Fulcio issues short-lived certificates, Rekor logs every signature, and verifiers check both.
The JSON envelope that holds a signature, its certificate and its transparency-log proof, pushed as a referrer.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework whose provenance format records how and where a package was built.
A `[[trust.policy]]` entry naming the signer identities OCX accepts for every package under one registry scope.
The Sigstore keys and certificates a verifier trusts: the Fulcio CA, the Rekor key and the CT log keys.
The Update Framework, the protocol Sigstore uses to distribute and rotate its trust root.
